statement: A rhombus has perimeter 40 cm and one diagonal 12 cm long. What is its area, in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I used half of the other diagonal, 8, in place of the whole 16, and worked out 12 x 8 / 2.
I treated the rhombus as a square of side 10 and worked out 10 x 10.
I multiplied the side 10 by the diagonal 12, as if the rhombus were a rectangle.
I multiplied the two diagonals, 12 x 16, and forgot to halve the product.

hints: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and cut each other in half.

The diagonals split the rhombus into four identical right triangles, each with a side as hypotenuse and half of each diagonal as legs. Find the missing half diagonal, then use the diagonals for the area.
Each side is 10 cm and half the known diagonal is 6 cm, so half the other diagonal is 8 cm.

solutions.reliable: Each side is 40 / 4 = 10 cm. The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so each of the four right triangles has hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6, which makes the other leg 8 (a 6-8-10 triangle). The other diagonal is therefore 16 cm. The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals: 12 x 16 / 2 = 96 square cm. The transferable idea: a rhombus is four identical right triangles, and its area is half the product of its diagonals.
solutions.elegant: Add up the four right triangles directly: each has legs 6 and 8, so each has area 6 x 8 / 2 = 24, and 4 x 24 = 96.

whyOnTest: Rhombus questions need two facts used together, perpendicular bisecting diagonals and Pythagoras, and the distractors catch anyone who uses only one of them.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
